items.stem: State how many electrons the first and second shells can each hold in the simplified model used for the first twenty elements.
items.modelAnswer: The first shell holds 2 electrons and the second holds 8 (and in this course the third shell is also treated as holding 8).

items.stem: Describe what the numbers in an electronic configuration such as 2,8,1 count.
items.modelAnswer: They count the electrons in each shell, separated by commas, counting from the nucleus outwards.

items.stem: Explain why potassium and calcium are described as breaking the simple filling pattern.
items.modelAnswer: Because their electrons enter the fourth shell before the third shell fills further — potassium's nineteenth electron starts the fourth shell, giving 2,8,8,1.

items.stem: A sodium atom has 11 electrons and forms an ion with a 1+ charge by losing its single outer electron. State how many occupied shells the ion has and the electrons in its outer shell.
items.modelAnswer: Two occupied shells with 8 electrons in the outer shell — the configuration is 2,8.

items.stem: State what the last number in an electronic configuration shows.
items.modelAnswer: It shows the number of outer electrons, and that count gives the group.

items.stem: State how to read an element's period from its electronic configuration.
items.modelAnswer: Count the number-groups in the configuration — the number of occupied shells equals the period.

items.stem: Explain why the exam Periodic Table alone does not give an element's period directly.
items.modelAnswer: Because the table prints the group number but not the period number, so you must label the period yourself from the occupied-shell count.

items.stem: Element X sits in the same group as chlorine, whose configuration is 2,8,7. State how many outer-shell electrons an atom of X has.
items.modelAnswer: Seven — atoms in the same group share their count of outer-shell electrons, so X has 7 outer electrons like chlorine.

items.stem: State which element is the exception to the group-number rule, and what its outer shell holds.
items.modelAnswer: Helium — it sits in Group 0 with just two electrons in its only shell.

items.stem: State how reactivity changes as you go down Group 7.
items.modelAnswer: It decreases — Group 7 elements turn less reactive further down the group.

items.stem: Explain why the group number works as a shorthand for how an element will react and bond.
items.modelAnswer: Because the group number equals the outer-shell electron count, and the outer electrons are the ones that take part in reactions and bonding.

items.stem: A student observes that bromine, a Group 7 element, reacts with potassium. State what this one observation predicts about chlorine and iodine.
items.modelAnswer: As members of the same group they are predicted to react in a similar way — observing one member of a group lets you predict how its partners react.

items.stem: State how the noble gases exist as elements: how many atoms each particle holds, what they look like, and their flammability.
items.modelAnswer: They are monatomic (single atoms), colourless non-metal gases, and they do not catch fire at room temperature.

items.stem: State which noble gas has the configuration 2,8,8, and what that configuration shows about its third shell.
items.modelAnswer: Argon — 2,8,8 shows a full third shell in this model, which is why argon sits inert in Group 0.

items.stem: Explain why noble gases need not lose, gain or share electrons.
items.modelAnswer: Because their outer shells are already full, so they have no need to lose, gain or share electrons to reach a stable arrangement.

items.stem: A newly discovered element is suspected to be a noble gas. State how many outer electrons it must carry (helium excepted), and what that predicts about the molecules it forms.
items.modelAnswer: Eight outer electrons — a full outer shell — so it will not form molecules easily.

items.stem: State where to find an element's relative atomic mass on the Periodic Table.
items.modelAnswer: It is the larger of the two numbers beside the element's symbol.

items.stem: State the other name for the relative formula mass when the substance is a simple molecule.
items.modelAnswer: The relative molecular mass.

items.stem: Explain why a balanced equation's two sides always carry the same mass.
items.modelAnswer: Because mass is conserved — balancing only rearranges atoms into new arrangements, so the totals on each side match.

items.stem: In the reaction N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, work out the total relative formula mass on each side (N 14, H 1) and state what the comparison shows.
items.modelAnswer: Reactants: N2 = 2 x 14 = 28 and 3H2 = 3 x 2 = 6, total 34; products: 2NH3 = 2 x 17 = 34 — the totals are equal, exactly what conservation of mass requires.

items.stem: State the effect of a subscript written after a closing bracket in a formula.
items.modelAnswer: It multiplies every element inside that bracket.

items.stem: State the fastest guard against miscounting bracketed groups.
items.modelAnswer: List the atoms present element by element before adding anything up.

items.stem: Explain why calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2, contains two oxygens rather than one.
items.modelAnswer: Because the subscript 2 after the bracket multiplies every element inside it — the single OH group becomes two O and two H.

items.stem: A student lists ammonium sulfate, (NH4)2SO4, element by element as N: 2 x 14, H: 8 x 1, S: 1 x 32, O: 4 x 16. State the four sub-totals and the Mr they add up to.
State step one of the three-step reacting mass method.
items.modelAnswer: Change the given mass into moles by dividing it by the relative formula mass.

items.stem: State what the moles from step two are multiplied by in the final step, and what that produces.
items.modelAnswer: The relative formula mass — multiplying the moles by it changes the answer back into a mass.

items.stem: Explain why the balancing numbers in the equation are needed in step two of the method.
items.modelAnswer: Because the balancing numbers give the molar ratio — the proportion in which the two substances react — and that ratio converts the moles of one substance into the moles of the other.

items.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Starting from 50 g of calcium carbonate (Mr 100), state the moles of calcium carbonate and the mass of calcium oxide (Mr 56) formed.
items.modelAnswer: Moles of CaCO3 = 50 / 100 = 0.5 mol; the ratio is 1 : 1, so 0.5 mol of CaO forms; mass = 0.5 x 56 = 28 g.

items.stem: State what every mole value is divided by to expose the whole-number ratio.
items.modelAnswer: By the smallest mole value of the set.

items.stem: State what can be added to the equation once each substance's physical state is known.
items.modelAnswer: The state symbols.

items.stem: Explain why each measured mass must be converted to moles before the ratio is taken.
items.modelAnswer: Because the equation's balancing numbers compare amounts in moles, not masses — converting to moles puts every substance on a comparable footing before the ratio is read.

items.stem: An experiment burns 1.2 g of magnesium (Ar 24) in 0.8 g of oxygen (Ar 16). Show the two mole results and state the whole-number Mg : O ratio and the formula it gives.
items.modelAnswer: Mg: 1.2 / 24 = 0.05 mol; O: 0.8 / 16 = 0.05 mol; dividing by the smallest gives 1 : 1, so the formula is MgO.

items.stem: State what the yield of a reaction describes.
items.modelAnswer: The yield is the amount of product obtained from a reaction.

items.stem: State what a side reaction is.
items.modelAnswer: When something extra reacts — such as a gas from the air, or an impurity mixed into a reactant.

items.stem: Explain why the mass of dry product weighed at the end is usually less than the reaction could have made.
items.modelAnswer: Because some reactant stays behind in the equipment and some product is lost during separation, purification and transfer between containers.

items.stem: State the two directions a reversible reaction keeps running in, and what that does to the amount of product that can build up.
items.modelAnswer: Products keep turning back into reactants as reactants keep forming products — because the products never all survive, a high yield is never possible.

items.stem: State the percentage yield sum in words.
items.modelAnswer: Divide the actual yield by the theoretical yield, then multiply by one hundred.

items.stem: State how each method of making a compound is described, and what it is built from.
items.modelAnswer: It is a reaction pathway — a route built from a sequence of reactions.

items.stem: Explain what a percentage yield above one hundred percent signals, and name the usual mistake behind it.
items.modelAnswer: It signals an error — usually the theoretical yield was divided by the actual yield, the inverse of the correct sum.

items.stem: A factory route delivers 31 g of product where the theoretical yield is 40 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
State the raw material a formula-by-experiment working starts from.
items.modelAnswer: Mass measurements taken before and after the reaction.

items.stem: Name the three kinds of compound the note says can have their formulae found experimentally.
items.modelAnswer: Metal oxides, water, and salts holding water of crystallisation.

items.stem: Explain why the before-and-after masses must be converted into moles before the formula can be deduced.
items.modelAnswer: Because formulae are ratios of atoms, and moles count particles — converting the masses into moles turns the data into the molar ratio that gives the empirical formula.

items.stem: Two experiments are planned: one where a gas escapes from an open crucible, and one where everything stays as solids in a sealed vessel. State which suits the mass-change method better, and why.
items.modelAnswer: The gas-escape experiment — experiments where a gas is lost or gained are the easiest to handle, because the mass change is easy to see.

items.stem: State the aim of the hydrated copper sulfate experiment in formula form.
items.modelAnswer: To determine the formula of hydrated copper sulfate, written CuSO4.xH2O.

items.stem: State why the salt must not be overheated.
items.modelAnswer: A decomposed salt loses extra mass, and that extra loss corrupts the water-to-salt ratio.

items.stem: Explain why the water's mass in this experiment is found by subtraction.
items.modelAnswer: Because heating drives the water off as steam — the hydrated mass minus the anhydrous mass left in the dish is exactly the water's contribution.

items.stem: A dish holds 2.50 g of hydrated salt; after gentle heating, 1.60 g of anhydrous solid remains. State the mass of water driven off.
